title: After the resuscitation
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in the Emergency Department. Half an hour ago, the team tried for 40 minutes to resuscitate a three-year-old, but the child died.

You find Maya, a nurse who was part of the team, crying in the sluice. She says she's fine and needs to get back to her patients. The department is busy.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Stay with Maya for a few minutes and ask how she is.
options.brief: A moment of genuine attention helps, even if she says she's fine.
options.detailed: After a child's death, many staff say they are fine when they aren't. Staying briefly and asking gently shows care and gives her a chance to talk if she wants to.

options.text: Tell her it gets easier with time.
options.brief: Well meant, but it can minimise what she is feeling now.
options.detailed: Some staff find this reassuring, but it may suggest her reaction is a sign of inexperience. Listening is more helpful than advice.

options.text: Leave her to compose herself, as she has said she's fine.
options.brief: Respects her words but may leave her unsupported.
options.detailed: Respecting her wishes matters, but a brief check costs little and may help. Leaving immediately could feel like nobody noticed.

options.text: Suggest she goes home for the rest of the shift.
options.brief: May not be what she wants, and it isn't your decision.
options.detailed: Some staff need to go home, but she wants to continue, and staffing decisions sit with the nurse in charge. Sending her home could feel like a judgement on her ability.

options.text: Ask the nurse in charge if Maya can have a short break.
options.brief: Practical support from the person who manages the workload.
options.detailed: The nurse in charge can cover her patients for a short while. A break may help her recover enough to work safely, and it avoids her feeling she has to ask.

options.text: Organise a formal debrief for the whole team yourself this afternoon.
options.brief: Debriefs are valuable, but they are usually led by senior staff.
options.detailed: A debrief may help, but organising it yourself, at short notice and without the senior team, may not be appropriate or effective.

options.brief: Premature and not your role at this stage.
options.detailed: Occupational health may help if distress continues, but a referral now, without her agreement, would be disproportionate.

options.text: Tell her about the team debrief and staff support services.
options.brief: She may want support later, even if not now.
options.detailed: Many departments hold debriefs after a child's death and offer staff support. Knowing what's available means she can use it when she's ready.

explanation.issue: This tests how you support a colleague after a traumatic event, balancing her wishes with care and practical help.
explanation.keyDetails: She has just been through a child's death. She says she's fine. The department is busy. She wants to keep working.
explanation.reasoning: [A] offers personal support, [E] arranges practical support, and [H] points to longer-term help. The distractors minimise ([B]), withdraw ([C]), override her ([D]), overstep ([F]), or escalate prematurely ([G]).
explanation.competing: [C] is tempting because she said she's fine, but a brief, gentle check is unlikely to be unwelcome and may matter a great deal.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, supporting colleagues and contributing to a supportive culture.
